title: GPX Speed / Pace Helper: Moving-Time Pace
description: Read a GPX track's pace from its moving time with the GPX Speed / Pace Helper — distance and pace, computed offline in your browser. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, 10 kilometres covered in 50 minutes of moving time is a 5:00-per-kilometre pace and a 12.0 km/h speed — the same performance wearing the runner's unit and the cyclist's unit.
quick_answer: The GPX Speed / Pace Helper loads a GPX track, reads its distance, and computes pace from your moving time. Drop the file — arithmetic happens offline in your browser — and read pace and speed, the two dialects of one performance.
steps_intro: Pace is speed in runner's clothing. Both, from the file:

body.t: The number runners actually trade in — minutes per kilometre — from the recording, with the
's elapsed figure beside it for the stop-inclusive truth.
A 3:30 marathon is 4:59 per kilometre at 12.06 km/h. Knowing your file's pace is knowing whether the goal pace is a plan or a hope.
Cyclists quote km/h; runners quote pace. The helper is the phrasebook — one performance, both units, no mental division at kilometre 30.
Same route, two Sundays: moving pace separates fitness from traffic lights — the comparison elapsed averages cannot honestly make.
Pace (min/km) = 60 ÷ speed (km/h). At 12.0 km/h, pace is 5:00/km; at 10 km/h, 6:00/km; at 15 km/h, 4:00/km. The table below is this identity, tabulated — no other formula hides anywhere in pace.

10 km in 50 moving minutes is 5:00/km. Add a 6-minute café stop inside the same outing and elapsed pace becomes 5:36/km — both numbers true, answering different questions, which is why this page insists on naming its denominator.

popular_table.intro: The identity pace = 60 ÷ speed, at the values athletes actually meet.
popular_table.note: Per-mile paces use the exact mile (1.609344 km). A 3:30 marathon runs 4:59/km and 8:01/mile — the pair of numbers painted on a thousand pace bands.

faq: By the recording's own movement: intervals where the track actually progresses count; standstills do not. Any threshold a tool applies is a judgement — this page's framing keeps the denominator visible rather than pretending 'moving' is a physical constant.
Both units are offered — American runners pace by the mile, European runners and most of the world's races by the kilometre.
What if the file has no timestamps?
Pace needs time. A timeless file yields distance only — its geometry tools (stats, box, splits by distance) still work, and only the clock-dependent family falls silent.
Pace exists over intervals; single-point 'pace' is a short segment in disguise. The Maximum Speed tool reads the extreme segment; this helper reads the outing.
Yes — pace averages terrain away. Splitting by segment (the sequential checker's distances against the stamps) is how climb versus descent pace gets separated.
Indoor recordings carry time with little or no GPS distance; pace from them is the device's estimate, not geometry. This helper works from what the file's coordinates support.
Why is my helper pace faster than my platform's?
Different moving-time thresholds: platforms discard slow shuffling differently (a traffic-light creep counts here, vanishes there). Same file, declared denominators, honest disagreement.
